groundTruthNarrative: CSD's 95%-green dashboard is a gamed self-report. After the SVP's 2025-11-03 memo, any amber or red status meant the lead presenting personally to the SVP under a threat of 'leadership changes'. From 2026 a quarter of leads' and directors' bonuses depended on percent green. Green share jumped from 64% to 91% within two months, and no red has been reported since, while CSD's on-time rate in the independent Customer Success register stayed at about 36%. The audit found 4 of 6 'green' projects behind schedule, and customers discovered slippage first. CSD's 'waiting on Platform' delays are mostly self-inflicted: requests arrive with 6 days' notice and 58% need resubmission, while complete, early CSD requests are delivered on time as reliably as other divisions'. Platform does have a real but modest 2026 capacity shortfall (3 vacancies, 2 secondments) that slowed everyone by a few days and has partly recovered. Survey participation collapsed only in CSD. The memo and the CSD-only February layoffs are entangled as causes of the drop. Whether the SVP knowingly directed misreporting is not established.

answers.rationale: The independent audit found 4 of 6 randomly sampled 'green' projects 3-9 weeks behind baseline, with slippage visible for at least 4 weeks while the dashboard stayed green (E11). The Customer Success register, kept outside CSD, shows CSD meeting only 36% of commitments in 2026 with no improvement since 2025 (E5), and in 5 of 7 escalations customers found slippage while the project was green (E15). A lead confirms a 5-week-late project reported green (E12). The SVP dismisses the audit as an anecdote (E1). The small sample is a fair caveat, but four independent sources agree, so 'unknown' is not defensible.

The same Platform team serves FVD and WSD, who met 87% and 83% of commitments against CSD's 36% (E5). CSD's low rate predates the June 2026 capacity shortfall (2025-Q3 to 2026-Q2 all 33-44%; E5, E7). Within CSD, requests filed complete and at least 15 days ahead were delivered on time 87% of the time, about the same as other divisions. Late or incomplete requests were on time 31% of the time (E6). The 'platform dependency' attribution for 12 of 16 misses was entered by CSD's own account team (E5). The audit traced both Platform-blocked projects to CSD filing after its own integration start (E11; also E12).

There is a clear mechanism: amber or red means presenting personally to the SVP under a threat of 'leadership changes' (E3), and from 2026 a quarter of variable pay depends on the share of green reports (E4). Green share jumped from 64% to 91% within two months of the memo, and no red has been reported since 2025-12-05 (E2), while external outcomes did not improve (E5). The audit shows green status on projects that were behind (E11). Anonymous staff describe green-shifting (E10), a lead was told to keep a late project green (E12), and customers found slippage first (E15). Other explanations (genuinely better delivery, a measurement quirk) are ruled out by E5 and E11.

The capacity issue is real. Platform had 3 vacancies from June and 2 secondments from July to October, and median cycle time for complete requests rose from 8 to 11 days in Q3 before recovering to 9 (E7). Platform's head admits it (E8), and FVD saw a 3-4 day slowdown (E14). Other divisions' on-time rate dipped only from 89% to 79% (E5), and complete, early CSD requests still ran 8 of 10 on time in Q3 (E6). So the constraint is genuine but secondary. Contradicted is wrong because the slowdown is documented, and the claim is not just unknown because its size is measured.

Survey fatigue would be company-wide. The same vendor, questions and cadence were used everywhere, yet company participation stayed at 70-74% while CSD fell from 78% to 31% (E9). The fall is specific to CSD, and CSD-specific themes dominate the comments (E10).

The memo puts heavy pressure on staff but does not tell anyone to misreport (E3). The instruction to 'keep it green' came from a director, and the lead does not know whether it started with the SVP (E12). The SVP's direct report says he was surprised by the audit (E13), but that director is one of the three status reviewers in the SVP's own line (E2, E13) and is not independent. The SVP's statement that leads are professionals (E1) fits both sincere belief and pretence. Nothing supplied separates knowing direction from pressure-induced inflation that he did not see, so the claim is live but unestablished.

The shortfall began in June 2026 (E7). CSD's on-time rate was already 33-44% in every quarter from 2025-Q3 to 2026-Q2 and was 38% in Q3 (E5), so the low rate predates the shortfall and did not move with it. During Q3, CSD's complete, early requests were still delivered on time 8 of 10 times (E6). The shortfall slowed everyone modestly (E7, E14), but it does not account for CSD's low rate. That counts against the link as stated, so the answer is not association-only.

Temporal order: the memo (2025-11-03) came before green share jumping from 64% to 91% by 2025-12-31, and no red has been reported since 2025-12-05 (E2, E3). Mechanism: a red status means personal exposure and a threat of leadership changes, and the bonus later rewarded percent green (E3, E4). Covariation: green went up while external outcomes stayed flat (E5) and the audit found green-but-late projects (E11, E15). Rivals: real improvement is ruled out by E5 and E11. The February 2026 layoffs came after the jump, so they cannot explain its onset (E9). Staff describe the mechanism directly (E10, E12).

Participation fell after the memo (78% in 2025-10, then 49% in 2026-03; E9), so the two co-occur. But no survey ran between the memo and the CSD-only layoffs of 2026-02-12, which are an equally plausible cause of the drop (E9). The comments split between status-reporting fear (9) and the layoffs (6) (E10). The evidence cannot tell the two causes apart, so the link is not established as causal. It is not contradicted either.

Mechanism: each incomplete-spec return added a median 7 business days, and CSD gave a median 6 days' notice against 17-21 for other divisions (E6). Within-division covariation: complete, early CSD requests were 87% on time against 31% for the rest. Same team, same period, and a similar mix of integration work rule out Platform favouring other divisions or CSD work being harder (E6). The audit traced both Platform-blocked late projects to requests filed after the project's own integration start (E11). A lead confirms the pattern (E12), and FVD's own late filings produced its misses (E14). The status codes cannot be set without the requester's acknowledgement (E6), so Platform could not have gamed them.

This punishes the wrong party. CSD's misses come from its own late, incomplete requests and from status that hides slippage (E6, E11), not from Platform underperformance (E5). Taking 12 engineers from about 35 (E7) would cut capacity by about a third for FVD and WSD, which are delivering 83-87% (E5). Penalty SLAs would be measured against need-by dates that CSD sets late (E6). It would also confirm the inflated narrative to the executive team.

This targets the established mechanism. Status is subjective, set inside the SVP's line (E2), and rewarded by percent green (E4), and it diverges from reality (E11, E15). An objective, externally validated status plus a bonus based on the independent register, which the other divisions already use (E4, E5), removes both the incentive and the means to inflate. It does not depend on settling the SVP's intent (H6).

The capacity constraint is confirmed (E7, E8), so backfilling is reasonable, not premature. But it addresses a secondary issue: cycle time had already recovered to 9 days in October after the secondees returned (E7), other divisions were only modestly affected (E5, E14), and it would not change CSD's 36% on-time rate, which comes from late, incomplete filing and hidden slippage (E6). It is therefore not among the best actions.

Removing the SVP for misrepresentation would be justified if H6 (knowing direction) were confirmed. The evidence leaves that open: the director-level instruction has an unclear origin (E12), the director reports the SVP was surprised (E13), and the memo applies pressure without telling anyone to misreport (E3). Committing now goes beyond the evidence. It is not harmful outright, because the SVP did create the pressure regime (E3, E4), and further evidence could justify the action.

Anonymity is the protective control that brought out the green-shifting reports in a division whose participation has already fallen to 31% (E9). Staff say that reporting red led to someone being moved off an account (E10), and status reports are tied to threats of leadership changes (E3). Unmasking authors would expose them to that retaliation risk and further suppress the information the organization most needs.

Sources not controlled by CSD (the audit E11, the Customer Success register E5 and escalation log E15, and ticket data E6) independently establish inflated status, its mechanism (E2-E4) and the real driver of Platform-related delay. That is enough to commit to the status-and-incentive reform (A2). What remains unknown (the SVP's intent, the cause of the participation drop) bears on personnel decisions, not on that intervention.
